extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (investigators, trainees, and research development staff) preparing or resubmitting NIH proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on when and how to contact NIH Program Officers (POs) about grant applications: whom to contact, what materials and questions to send, appropriate topics at each stage, and Do/Don't principles for effective interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Program Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers read the study section's recommendations and make the final grant funding decisions — incorporating together: the score, the reviews (summary statement), and the ability of the grant to address the mission of the institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that POs synthesize score, reviewer comments, and mission-fit when making funding decisions; this frames what questions are useful to ask and what influence a PO realistically has.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Contact a Program Officer (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended contact points: Before submission (to discuss fit, get advice); After receiving summary statement (to discuss path forward); During grant preparation (with specific aims draft); For resubmission strategy (after rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POs are most supportive when contacted early in the proposal planning process — NOT 3-4 weeks before an NIH deadline. Contacting late is an anti-pattern; plan outreach well before submission deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Assistance POs Can Provide
rubrics_metrics.description: POs can provide general tips and strategies on writing strong applications; greater clarity on reviewer critiques; areas of focus for a potential resubmission; guidance on whether your project fits the institute's mission; information on RFA opportunities; insight into funding outlook; and information on the peer review meeting (if they attended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use POs for strategic, programmatic, and interpretive advice (fit, review interpretation, opportunities). Ask them clarifying and planning questions rather than seeking to change reviewer judgments or guarantee outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on What POs Can Do
rubrics_metrics.description: POs cannot influence individual reviewer scores; cannot guarantee funding; cannot share confidential review discussions; cannot lobby reviewers on your behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame requests recognizing these limits. Avoid asking POs to take actions they cannot (or should not) perform, such as intervening with reviewers or assuring funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email Best Practices (how to compose inquiries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose your inquiry concisely with: Your name; Reason for contacting them; Your years in the lab/career stage; The grant you are applying for; Specific question(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POs receive many emails a day — be concise and specific. Lead with the purpose and include career context and the specific funding mechanism to help the PO triage and respond quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Materials to Send
rubrics_metrics.description: Research Development recommends: develop ideas in form of a draft Specific Aims page; email to the program officer; 1-page summary of the project; your CV/biosketch; specific questions you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide succinct, targeted materials (aims page, 1-page summary, biosketch) and concrete questions so the PO can give informed, actionable feedback. Avoid sending overly long drafts without a clear question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phone vs. Email Protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Email first to set up phone discussion if needed; phone calls are appropriate for nuanced discussions; don't cold-call; schedule via email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use email to request and schedule calls. Reserve phone conversations for complex or sensitive topics; do not cold-call POs as an initial contact method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and Choosing the Right Program Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: After review, the PO is listed on your eRA Commons account. Before submission, find PO based on: your scientific area within an institute; names of POs on similar funded grants (NIH RePORTER); institute's program staff page. Multiple institutes may be relevant — match your project to the institute mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the PO whose portfolio/mission aligns best with your proposal; check eRA Commons, NIH RePORTER, and institute staff pages. Consider multiple institutes if applicable and choose the best mission fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Discussion Topics — Pre-submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-submission topics include: Does this fit your institute's priorities? Is the right mechanism R01, R21, R03, K? What's the funding outlook? Any specific RFAs to consider? Should I contact a specific study section?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-submission conversations to confirm fit, choose the correct mechanism, identify RFAs or study sections, and gauge funding prospects. Bring draft aims or a 1-page summary to make the conversation concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Discussion Topics — Post-summary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-summary topics include: What did the panel discuss? How significant are the criticisms? Should I resubmit or move on? What's the realistic path to funding? Any administrative supplements available?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After review, ask POs to interpret the summary statement and help weigh resubmission vs. alternative strategies; inquire about realistic funding pathways and administrative opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Principles for Interacting with POs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be respectful of their time; Be concise; Be specific; Don't ask them to write your grant; Don't pressure or lobby; Build a long-term relationship — POs remember.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow etiquette: respect time, be concise and specific, avoid asking POs to draft or unduly influence review, and cultivate ongoing professional relationships rather than transactional one-off contacts.
